title: Global, regional and national burden of pertussis in 1990–2023: a Global Burden of Disease study
desc: Despite long-standing immunization programs, pertussis remains a major cause of vaccine-preventable mortality, particularly among infants. Here we present a primary assessment of global pertussis incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life years across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. We show that despite short-term pandemic-period fluctuations, the dominant global pattern from 1990 to 2023 was long-term decline: age-standardized mortality decreased by 61.2% and age-standardized incidence by 41.6%. Relative to the anomalously low pandemic-period estimates, incidence and mortality rebounded by 102.6% (95% uncertainty interval, 77.0–128.2%) and 66.1% (95% uncertainty interval, 2.4–174.5%), respectively, between 2020 and 2023. In 2023 alone, we estimated 18.9 million cases and 115,000 deaths attributable to pertussis. This burden remains profoundly inequitable and inversely correlated with the sociodemographic index; sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for roughly 65% of global deaths, with the highest population-adjusted risk concentrated among infants younger than 6 months. Our findings highlight a modeled geographic concentration of pertussis mortality and support strengthening timely infant vaccination, maternal immunization where recommended and feasible and robust surveillance in highly susceptible regions. Updates to the Global Burden of Disease study showed that while global trends in pertussis (whooping cough) declined from 1990 to 2023, the rebound in incidence and mortality since 2020, particularly in high-income regions, reflects stalled vaccination progress worldwide.

title: Agentic artificial intelligence for code status extraction from clinical notes: a cross-model comparison of single agent, reflective agent, and multiagent extractor-reviewer system.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To evaluate whether increasing agentic architectural complexity via self-reflection or multiagent design improves clinical code status extraction (Do Not Resuscitate [DNR], Do Not Intubate [DNI], Comfort Measures Only [CMO]) across open-source large language models (LLMs) of varying capabilities. We conducted a controlled cross-model comparison evaluating 3 architectures: (1) single extractor agent, (2) single agent with self-reflection, and (3) sequential multiagent extractor-reviewer system. Four open-source LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B) were evaluated on 1000 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV-Note discharge summaries. Ground truth labels were established through a physician-AI dual review with adjudication (Cohen's κ = 0.98-0.99). Models were evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Cohen's κ, token consumption, and processing latency. McNemar's test was used for paired comparisons. For capable larger models (GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B), single-agent architectures achieved comparable or superior performance for explicit code status (DNR, DNI) relative to complex systems, whereas multiagent review doubled token consumption and latency without accuracy gains. Reflective self-review significantly impaired MedGemma-27B-IT on DNI extraction (P = .047). For the smaller DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, multiagent review provided statistically significant corrective benefits for DNR (P = .017) and CMO (P < .001), demonstrating a capability-threshold effect, though performance remained below clinically acceptable levels. Architectural complexity does not enhance extraction performance for capable LLMs, and reflective self-review may cause conservative overcorrection. Multiagent verification value is inversely related to model capability. Single-agent LLMs provide optimal accuracy and efficiency for explicit clinical extraction in capable models. Agentic complexity must be matched to both task characteristics and model capability rather than adopted by default.

title: Silent evaluation reveals context-dependent validity of automated metrics for AI-generated clinical messages
desc: Evaluation of AI-generated patient communication lacks standardized frameworks, and automated metrics may not reflect clinical utility. We leveraged a staged rollout of GPT-generated draft responses (GDRs) to patient portal messages. Thirty primary care physicians received drafts from September 2023 to August 2024 under two conditions: an intervention group where AI drafts were displayed and edited ( n = 21,073), and a non-displayed group where drafts were generated but never shown to physicians, who composed responses independently ( n = 45,127). We evaluated messages using BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, and Flesch Reading Ease, and then correlated automated metrics with blinded physician ratings of effectiveness, misunderstanding potential, and harm. In the intervention group, 2264 (11%) drafts were incorporated into final messages with high semantic alignment (BERTScore F1 = 0.93). In the non-displayed group, independent physician messages showed moderate similarity to unseen drafts (BERTScore F1 = 0.83). Despite comparable semantic scores, physicians preferred human-authored messages (4.24/5). BERTScore correlated with physician quality ratings in the intervention group but not in the non-displayed. Automated metrics demonstrated context-dependent validity; they assessed editing fidelity but failed to evaluate whether AI-generated content matches independent human performance. Rigorous evaluation of clinical generative AI requires validation of metric meaning within specific use contexts.

title: Rediscovering medical humanism in the age of artificial intelligence: lessons from historical medical traditions.
source: PubMed · Clinical & translational oncology : official publication of the Federation of Spanish Oncology Societies and of the National Cancer Institute of Mexico
desc: [Clinical & translational oncology : official publication of the Federation of Spanish Oncology Societies and of the National Cancer Institute of Mexico] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming diagnosis, treatment selection, prognostic assessment, and administrative work in medicine. Although these technologies may improve efficiency and clinical performance, their integration also raises questions about medical humanism, professional responsibility, and the physician-patient relationship. This narrative historical review examines the contributions of Hippocrates, Asclepiades, Galen, Avicenna, and Maimonides to the relationship between medical knowledge, clinical judgment, and moral responsibility, and considers how these historical traditions may inform contemporary debates on AI in medicine and oncology. Primary historical texts and secondary scholarly literature were examined through a targeted, non-systematic approach, with emphasis on clinical observation, therapeutic responsibility, the physician-patient relationship, and the ethical purposes of medicine. The analysis identifies three normative themes of contemporary relevance: the non-delegable responsibility of the physician, the relational and contextual nature of clinical reasoning, and the ethical limits of technological optimization. Contemporary philosophy of medicine and recent AI ethics literature provide a conceptual bridge between these historical traditions and current technological practice. This bridge might be the source of a lack of humanism in daily practice and a deterioration in patient-physician relationship. In oncology, these principles related to AI use are particularly relevant to AI-assisted imaging and pathology, molecular profiling, treatment selection, prognostic prediction, and shared decision-making. AI should, therefore, be understood as a clinical instrument whose value depends not only on technical performance, but also on its integration into relationships of trust, accountability, and patient-centered care.

title: AI-Based CT Analysis of Coronary Plaque Evolution
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Zhejiang Hospital; conditions: Coronary Artery Disease; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 326; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This retrospective, multicenter, observational study will evaluate an artificial intelligence-based system for quantitative assessment and risk stratification of coronary atherosclerotic plaque. Adults with coronary plaque on baseline coronary CT angiography (CCTA) and at least one follow-up CCTA obtained between January 1, 2020 and December 31, 2025 will be identified from participating centers. The system will integrate clinical factors, CCTA plaque morphology and burden, functional measures, hemodynamic parameters, and biomechanical features using baseline data. Two independent readers will assess conventional CCTA findings, including CAD-RADS and adverse plaque characteristics, while remaining blinded to system outputs. The primary outcome is patient-level definite progression of non-calcified plaque, defined by annualized change in non-calcified plaque percent atheroma volume exceeding the reproducibility-based minimum detectable change (MDC95). Model discrimination will be assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and compared with conventional CCTA models. Approximately 326 participants are planned.

title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
desc: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

title: AI-Empowered Multimodal Data Integration and Knowledge Discovery for Pharmacovigilance
desc: Biomedical artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on heterogeneous data sources, yet differences in data structure, terminology, evidence quality, and provenance complicate their integration into reliable knowledge resources. Here, we develop an evidence-aware framework for processing and integrating heterogeneous pharmacovigilance data from FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reports, biomedical literature, clinical trials, and electronic health records in Mass General Brigham. The framework combines large language model (LLM)-based information extraction, ontology-driven semantic normalization, cross-source evidence assessment, statistical and machine learning-based prioritization, and ingredient-based adverse drug event (ADE) relationship inference to transform heterogeneous evidence into a structured and evidence-based knowledge resource. The constructed knowledge system contains 11,588 drug nodes, 44,843 ingredient nodes, 3,275 ADE nodes, 993 indication nodes, and more than 2.47 million relationships, with each drug-ADE relationship assigned a confidence score. We further developed a drug-level web interface for accessing the knowledge resource and validated its utility in downstream AI tasks. Specifically, incorporating the developed knowledge resource improved the comprehensiveness, relevance, and overall quality of LLM-based drug-specific ADE synthesis and improved the precision and F1 score of clinical ADE relation extraction. These results demonstrate that AI-assisted processing combined with evidence-aware curation can transform heterogeneous biomedical evidence into reusable, AI-ready knowledge with explicit provenance and evidence strength information. The framework provides a general strategy for integrating heterogeneous biomedical data to support reproducible knowledge construction and downstream biomedical AI applications.

title: An Evidence-Driven Multi-Agent Compound AI System for Head and Neck Proton Radiotherapy Planning
desc: Radiation treatment planning requires balancing competing objectives to satisfy clinical criteria while accommodating physicians' preferences. This study aims to develop an evidence-driven, multi-agent compound AI system that integrates DRL-based automated treatment planning with LLM-based conversational plan refinement for proton PBS therapy. A policy network trained using PPO first generates multiple plans without human intervention, from which one is selected as the target plan and the others serve as references for subsequent refinements. For challenging cases requiring further adjustments, an LLM-based multi-agent system enables plan refinement through natural language interactions. The system comprises a planning agent that recommends evidence-supported adjustments, a chatbot providing a unified conversational interface, and an evaluation agent that retrieves clinical metrics and identifies constraint violations. To enhance domain-specific reasoning, the planning agent based on Qwen3-14B is designed to justify its recommendations using evidence from previously generated plans and post-trained on task-specific data using SFT and GRPO. The framework was trained and evaluated using 21 patients with H&N cancers, with 5 PPO-generated plans per patient. Of these, 50 plans were selected for instruction-guided refinement. Compared with the base LLM, the post-trained Qwen3-14B demonstrated improved instruction-following, information retrieval and domain-specific reasoning capabilities. The resulting adjustments more effectively improved user-prioritized objectives while limiting deterioration in competing objectives, yielding more clinically appropriate trade-offs in patient-specific plan refinement. The proposed compound AI system provides a user-friendly planning platform, offering a promising approach to personalized proton PBS treatment planning.

title: GENOAR: Global Engine for Navigating the Omnicell space via Agent-based Research
desc: Although generative models have revolutionized many fields, including genomics, building a scalable dataset compatible with artificial intelligence (AI) is essential yet underexplored. Here, we developed a Global Engine for navigating the Omnicell space via Agent-based Research (GENOAR) that covers approximately 54 million cells for diverse downstream tasks using AI agents and parallel computing. GENOAR outperforms in three parts. Parallel computations accelerated the preprocessing of single-cell transcriptomic data; the other components enabled agent-assisted data storage and exploration for both AI models and humans. GENOAR involves two AI agents: an AI nomenclaturist ordered the unstructured labels of the single-cell transcriptomic profiles, and an AI librarian retrieved data. GENOAR presents transcriptomic profiles from more than 54 million cells from humans and mice in an analysis-ready format for humans and AI agents. AI agents in GENOAR exhibited successful retrieval performance compared with human experts. Using GENOAR, we elucidated progenitor cell-associated transcriptional signatures in native retinoblastoma and organoid environments. GENOAR was released and validated for the on-demand construction of single-cell atlases for metazoa. In conclusion, using GENOAR, the development of a single-cell transcriptomic atlas compatible with both AI systems and human researchers is feasible, scalable, and reproducible.

Global and regional burden of measles and vaccine coverage among children under 5 years, 1990−2023: a Global Burden of Disease Study
desc: Measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable burden among children, particularly in low-income settings. Despite decades of progress, there are indications of measles resurgence due to stagnation in vaccine coverage. Here, using the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, we systematically assessed measles incidence, mortality, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and vaccine coverage (measles-containing vaccine 1 (MCV1) and measles-containing vaccine 2 (MCV2)) among children under 5 years of age across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Between 1990 and 2019, global measles incidence and mortality declined by approximately 80% and 90%, respectively, but rebounded sharply after 2020, with 15.6 million cases and 118,000 deaths estimated in 2023 (+40% and +12% increases, respectively, between 2019 and 2023). Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia continue to bear the highest burden. Global MCV1 coverage rose from 67.2% in 1990 to 83.6% in 2019 but stalled and declined slightly to 81.0% by 2023; MCV2 coverage increased from 14.4% in 1990 to 68.4% in 2019 and reached 71.4% by 2023. Several regions remain well below the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030) target of 90% coverage. The recent measles resurgence underscores the fragility of global immunization progress and the urgent need to restore routine vaccination, close immunity gaps and strengthen outbreak preparedness. Updates to the Global Burden of Disease Study showed that although global measles incidence and mortality had declined in 1990−2019, its resurgence since 2020 reflects stalled vaccination progress worldwide.

title: Towards reliable morphological subtyping and cancer detection on Barrett’s esophagus pathology through ensembling foundation models
desc: The reliability of emergent histopathology foundation models (Histo-FMs) for real-world diagnostic tasks remains unproven. Given the complexity of diagnostic tasks and the challenges inherent in real-world data, we utilized Histo-FMs to investigate their utility for morphological subtyping of Barrett’s esophagus (BE) and detecting esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) across the BE progression spectrum. We benchmarked Histo-FMs on the BarrettNet cohort, spanning diagnostic categories ranging from normal to EAC (N2EAC). The dataset comprised 3528 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs) from 790 patients. A multi-magnification, multi-backbone aggregation of the five most expert-consistent single-scale models yielded incremental performance gains (AUROC of 0.907, F1-score of 0.696, accuracy of 0.795, and κ of 0.651 for morphological subtyping; AUROC of 0.909, F1-score of 0.836, accuracy of 0.959, and κ of 0.673 for EAC detection), with non-uniform gains across single-model comparisons and limited benefit for dysplasia. The findings support the capability of Histo-FMs for BE morphological subtyping and EAC detection in a multicenter clinical cohort, while highlighting persistent challenges in dysplasia assessment and the need for external validation. This study provides a foundation for future clinical validation.

title: Artificial intelligence decision support for breast ultrasound: potential to reduce benign biopsies.
source: PubMed · Breast cancer research and treatment
desc: [Breast cancer research and treatment] The purpose of this study is to evaluate the potential impact of a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound in reducing benign biopsies. This study was conducted at two academic medical centers from March to May 2025 following the clinical implementation of an FDA-cleared AI-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound interpretation (Koios DS; New York, NY). Fourteen breast imaging radiologists documented BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) cases, along with the corresponding AI output. AI assessments were compared with biopsy pathology results to characterize AI classification within this selected cohort. Overall, 271 lesions in 253 women (mean age, 54 years; range, 24-92 years) were categorized as BI-RADS 4 and were biopsied, aspirated, and/or surgically excised. Of these, 23.2% (63/271) yielded malignant pathology, while 76.8% (208/271) were benign. The AI tool classified 90.5% (57/63) of malignant lesions as BI-RADS 4 and 9.5% (6/63) as BI-RADS 2 or 3. Among benign cases, the AI tool assigned 41.8% (87/208) as BI-RADS 2 (benign), 18.8% (39/208) as BI-RADS 3 (probably benign), and 39.4% (82/208) as BI-RADS 4 (suspicious). Retrospective application of the AI output to biopsy triage decisions suggests the potential for reduction in benign biopsy recommendations, with 60.6% (126/208) of benign lesions classified by the AI tool as BI-RADS 2 or 3. AI may help reduce benign biopsy recommendations among lesions assessed as BI-RADS 4 by radiologists; however, careful integration with radiologist judgment and clinical history is essential to ensure timely cancer diagnosis.

title: What Should we Measure? A Qualitative Interview Study on Outcomes for Evaluating AI-assisted Medical Image Interpretation.
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University of Oxford; conditions: Artificial Intelligence Perception and Attitude; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 30; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] Background: AI (artificial intelligence) tools are increasingly used to help clinicians interpret medical images such as X-rays, scans, skin photographs and eye images. In most cases the AI does not work alone: a clinician makes the final decision, using the AI as support. Before these tools are used in the NHS, they must be tested to show they are safe and helpful. They are usually tested in a "reader study", where several clinicians each interpret the same set of images, sometimes with the AI's help and sometimes without, so performance can be compared. These studies tend to focus on whether the diagnosis was correct. However, accuracy alone may not measure everything that matters. For example, what happens when the AI gets it wrong, whether clinicians rely on it too much or too little, or how the tool affects efficiency. At present there is no agreed standard for what these studies should measure, so important things are often missed and studies are hard to compare. Aim: The aim of this study is to find out, by talking to people with different perspectives, which outcomes are important when evaluating AI tools that help clinicians read medical images. Objectives: 1. Explore which outcomes people think matter when judging whether an AI tools is safe and good enough to use 2. Understand the reasons behind their views 3. Explore how priorities differ between groups, such as patients and developers. The output will be a list of important candidate outcomes, which will feed into a future project to agree a recommended set of outcomes for these studies (a "core outcome set"). Research value: Without agreement on what to measure, studies of AI tools may overlook outcomes that matter, and their results are difficult to compare and combine. Hearing directly from the people affected, rather than relying only on what previous studies happened to measure, helps ensure the recommended set reflects people's priorities. This will lead to better-designed studies and AI tools that are safer and more useful in practice. title: HarnessRL: Co-Evolving Policies with a Just-in-Time Training Harness for Open-Ended RL
desc: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies for open-ended generation with natural-language criteria as rewards, but these rewards can become ineffective as training progresses. We identify two failure modes. Under non-discriminative rewards, scores collapse to uniformly low or high values due to insufficient exploration or a mismatch between task difficulty and policy capability. Under spurious rewards, higher scores do not correspond to better responses. Both reflect a training configuration whose task sampling, exploration, and evaluation stay fixed as the policy evolves. We introduce HarnessRL, a training-time harness that co-evolves with the policy through three interfaces for task sampling, rollout guidance, and rubric criteria. HarnessRL maintains a training-time memory from which a harness evolver retrieves within-task history and cross-task evidence. Using this evidence, the evolver attributes each reward failure to the interface whose update can address it. It then runs a proposer and just-in-time critic loop in which the critic accepts a candidate update only after measuring its effect on the current frozen policy, returning rejected candidates for revision. We also curate Rubric-Mix-10k, a five-domain training and evaluation suite for open-ended RL across medical, science, writing, role-play, and instruction-following tasks. On Rubric-Mix-10k, HarnessRL outperforms the strongest baselines by 2.8 to 3.1 points across both 4B and 9B model scales and nearly halves the training steps to its best checkpoint. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Tongyi-ConvAI/Qwen-Character/tree/main/HarnessRL.

title: Design and Technical Evaluation of a Standards-Based System That Delivers Enclave-Derived Case-Finding Models to Patients and Clinicians
desc: Background. Research data enclaves such as the All of Us Research Program do not allow participant-level data, or models fitted to them, to leave, which makes it hard to deliver case-finding models, which flag patients with possibly uncoded conditions for clinician review, to patients and clinicians. Objectives. We describe and technically evaluate a system that fits models outside an enclave from released summary counts and delivers them through standard health information technology interfaces. Methods. We exported dissemination-compliant summary counts from the All of Us Researcher Workbench and, outside the enclave, fitted versioned models for Long COVID, chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, endometriosis, Lyme disease, lupus, migraine, depression, and anxiety. A model contract (a model file and a written specification), a Python reference implementation, and synthetic Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) test patients define the expected outputs. One JavaScript scorer runs in a patient demonstration, a SMART on FHIR clinician application, and a CDS Hooks service. An atlas displays aggregate results. We evaluated the system on synthetic records with automated tests, cross-implementation output comparison, launches through the public SMART sandbox, and a counterexample review of the scoring and display rules. Results. The deployed Long COVID model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.67 in a random validation split. The eight self-report models reached 0.61 to 0.82 in identifying self-reporters without a code. The JavaScript scorer reproduced all 162 reference outputs exactly, and all 437 automated tests passed. A counterexample review found 5 classes of failure, including scoring ineligible patients and treating unavailable data as absent, all fixed and added as tests. Conclusions. Models fitted from released summary counts can be delivered through FHIR, SMART on FHIR, and CDS Hooks with reproducible scoring on synthetic records. Real-record interoperability, usability, and prospective clinical performance remain to be evaluated.

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis
desc: Deep learning has become the default tool for medical image analysis, driven by the open-source movement. However, achieving the best performance on a given task remains difficult, with architecture selection and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) still considered "more of an art than a science". Automated machine learning (AutoML) automates parts of model training, yet helps little in medical imaging: general-purpose approaches lack medical architectures and preprocessing, and medical-focused ones demand engineering expertise and remain confined to narrow tasks such as 3D segmentation. We introduce MedicalMLOmni, a multi-agent AutoML framework that automates model training for diverse single- and multi-modal medical tasks through a natural language interface. Specifically, MedicalMLOmni performs evidence-based planning by retrieving published results to guide model selection and configuration, and employs parallel HPO where multiple agents explore adjustment strategies concurrently. MedicalMLOmni achieves the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks; PMC-VQA is the exception, where a vision-language model with broader pre-training leads. Backbone-matched controls attribute the gains to the framework, not the backbone. By removing coding requirements, MedicalMLOmni lowers the barrier for domain experts with rich datasets but limited engineering expertise.

title: Contextual Biomedical Language Models for Imbalance-Aware Drug-Food Interaction Classification
desc: Drug-food interactions (DFIs) are essential to patient safety because they can alter drug effectiveness or cause side effects. Automated classification of DFIs is difficult because of unstructured textual data, semantic ambiguity, and class imbalance, especially when separating neutral interactions. This paper presents an imbalance-aware deep learning approach for classifying drug-food interactions into three classes: safe, neutral, and unsafe. A structured dataset is created from textual drug interaction descriptions by extracting drug-food pairs and labeling them using rule-based heuristics. To address class imbalance, we apply class weighting and focal loss while fine-tuning the context-aware BioBERT language model. Our experiments show that the approach reaches an accuracy of 85% and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.77, with a notable improvement on the minority neutral class (F1-score of 0.56). The main novelty of this work is the combination of contextual biomedical language modeling with imbalance-aware deep learning, enabling more effective classification of DFI datasets.

title: A Generative AI-powered navigation system for precision CBCT-guided lung biopsies: a randomized controlled trial
desc: Lung puncture biopsy is the gold standard for the qualitative diagnosis of lung nodules. Cone Beam CT (CBCT) is commonly used for guiding punctures to locate lung nodules. However, the poor quality of CBCT images and the limited intelligence of surgical guidance systems have lowered the efficiency of puncture procedures, particularly for small and complex lesions. This study developed and validated a robust and accurate Generative AI-Powered Puncture Surgery Navigation System for lung punctures (GPS-Lung), demonstrating clinical applicability through a multicenter randomized controlled trial (Registration number: NCT06762613). The clinical results showed significant improvements in surgeon performance with the assistance of the integrated GPS-Lung system. Specifically, the system facilitated a more standardized and efficient operational process, reducing number of punctures (2.0 ± 1.2 vs. 2.5 ± 1.7, P = 0.005), shortening operative time (20.4 ± 5.6 min vs. 23.2 ± 6.3 min, P = 0.001), decreasing radiation exposure (4357.4 ± 3427.3 μGy·m^2 vs. 5570.9 ± 4846.7 μGy·m^2, P = 0.033), and reducing pneumothorax complications (12.7% vs. 23.9%, P = 0.033). Taken together, the proposed system demonstrates promising clinical and translational value in lung nodule puncture intervention. (Clinical Trials Registration: NCT06762613). title: Training the Next Generation of Future Surgical Residents: A Scoping Review and Proposal for an Undergraduate Curriculum From the Italian Polispecialistic Society of Young Surgeons.
desc: [Annali italiani di chirurgia] The transition from medical school to surgical residency is marked by a persistent gap between theoretical instruction and clinical readiness. In Italy, variability in training programs across centers creates persistent gaps in residents' medical education. Scientific societies are asked to identify current training gaps and define the core competencies required for effective surgical training. We propose an undergraduate curriculum to support last-year medical students in Italy. A scoping review of the literature focusing on structured surgical curricula for undergraduate medical students was conducted. A suggested "curriculum" was introduced at the 2025 Congress of the Italian Polispecialistic Society of Young Surgeons (SPIGC) in Bari, Italy. The SPIGC curriculum includes seven domains: (1) soft skills: communication, informed consent, and interdisciplinary collaboration; (2) clinical and diagnostic skills: outpatient clinic management and perioperative care; (3) hygiene, prevention, healthcare systems; (4) technical skills; (5) emergency and trauma surgery; (6) perioperative management, integrating Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols, nutritional assessment, and infections; (7) evidence-based medicine and recommendations. The SPIGC curriculum highlights the importance of simulation labs, hands-on workshops, and online learning, while providing clear pathways for fellowships or masters. It also introduces artificial intelligence (AI) systems as a modern learning tool, while highlighting the importance of their safe and responsible use. The SPIGC curriculum may provide a structured plan to improve surgical education for medical students in Italy and to align it with international standards. Its acceptability and impact on training quality and patient outcomes remain to be evaluated through future consensus and prospective studies.

title: Chatbot Utilization for Pedigree Creation and Cancer Risk Assessment in Cancer Genetic Counseling
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Roswell Park Cancer Institute; conditions: Hereditary Breast Carcinoma, Hereditary Malignant Neoplasm; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 129; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This clinical trial studies whether a chatbot can be used to help collect medical history and perform cancer risk assessment among patients undergoing cancer genetic counseling. With the improved cost of genetic testing and growing utilization of genetics in cancer care and risk assessment, there is growing pressure placed on certified genetic counselors. To address this issue, many have turned to artificial intelligence (the branch of computer science that deals with writing computer programs that can solve problems creatively) for practical solutions to re-distribute the workload of certified genetic counselors. The chatbot in this trial uses artificial intelligence technology to analyze information provided by the patient during a phone call. The chatbot then generates a family history summary, family tree (pedigree), and cancer risk related assessments, which may help redistribute the workload for the certified genetic counselor and ultimately make genetic counseling more accessible. Using a chatbot may be helpful in collecting medical history and determining cancer risk assessment among patients undergoing cancer genetic counseling.

title: Parental Health Information Needs, Child-Health Literacy, and Use of Generative AI Among Parents of Children Aged 0 to 4 Years in France: A Cross-Sectional Study
desc: Background: The first thousand days are a sensitive window for child health and social health inequalities. When routine care falls short, parents of young children turn to online sources and, recently, to generative artificial intelligence (AI). Evidence on their concerns, child-health literacy, and AI use is scarce. Objective: To describe health informational needs and concerns, child-health literacy, and use of AI for child-health questions, including differences by parental role and parity, among parents of young children. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, two anonymous self-administered online questionnaires were disseminated through a digital health application between May 12 and June 11, 2026, to French-speaking parents of at least one child aged 0 to 47 months in France. Questionnaire 1 covered unmet information needs, concerns across 16 topics, perceived intra-couple concordance, and confidence in routine care. Questionnaire 2 covered a four-item child-health literacy quiz and AI use (frequency, topics, 12-month trend, barriers, trust conditions, perceived effect on consultations, and disclosure). Results: In total, 12,634 parents responded (Questionnaire 1, n=5,410; Questionnaire 2, n=7,224), mostly mothers (94.6% and 92.9%). Most (61.8%) had searched for information without finding a clear, reliable answer, selecting a median of 4 (Interquartile range [IQR] 3-7) over 16 topics. Leading concerns were sleep (51.3%), nutrition (48.1%), and education (i.e., upbringing and behavior) (47.8%). Mothers were nearly twice as likely as fathers to select accident prevention (26.5% vs 16.3%) and parental mental health (38.7% vs 28.6%); first-time parents selected most topics more often than experienced parents, most markedly dental hygiene (43.8% vs 27.6%). The median child-health literacy score was 3 (IQR 3-4) on a 0-to-4 quiz, with 19.9% of parents scoring 2 or below; tooth-brushing age was the weakest item (68.4% correct). Mothers outscored fathers on every item. More than half of parents (54.2%) had used AI for a child-health question, 11.2% weekly; among those reporting a trend, 68.3% had increased AI use for child-health questions over the year and 6.2% decreased it. The main barriers to AI use were a preference for professionals (55.9%) and reliability concerns (48.7%); trust depended most on medical oversight of the tool (76.6%). title: MedBOE: Optimization-Based Estimation of Complete Patient Body Models from Whole-Body Medical Imaging
desc: True whole-body medical imaging captures a patient from head to toe and provides comprehensive anatomical and/or functional information. This coverage enables reconstruction of the external body surface, yielding patient body models. However, scanner geometry (e.g., bore diameter), patient characteristics, and positioning can leave body regions missing (e.g., lateral arms/torso, hands, forearms, elbows), producing incomplete patient body models. Such incompleteness limits downstream medical analyses, including derivation of body-habitus metrics (BHMs), such as body volume and surface area, for injected radiotracer activity regimens, cardiometabolic risk assessment, and computational anatomical modeling for medical imaging simulation and radiation dosimetry. We present the Medical Body model Optimization-based Estimator (MedBOE), an automated, training-free framework for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions. Our innovation is to leverage the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) template, a parametric body mesh representing a broad range of body shapes and poses, in medical imaging. MedBOE aligns the SMPL template to the incomplete patient body models via attribute-guided optimization and estimates missing body regions through geometrically and volumetrically constrained deformation. We evaluated MedBOE using two public datasets: AutoPET (91 whole-body PET-CT images) and Human Implicit Tissues (HIT; 40 whole-body segmentations from MRI images). MedBOE achieved the best overall volumetric and geometric performance among evaluated methods. BHMs derived from MedBOE were within 2% error, suggesting low percentage errors for downstream analyses. MedBOE offers an automated, training-free method for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions.

title: hvantk: an agentic multi-omics framework for variant annotation and analysis
desc: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their versions. Here, we present hvantk, a framework that provides a common data model for large-scale annotation and analysis of genetic variants, by extending popular data formats such as Hail MatrixTable and AnnData. hvantk agentically integrates 21 public multi-omic data providers as plugins that a developer, bioinformatician or an AI agent can author without modifying the framework's core, drives analysis workflows using agent skills, and scales from single desktop computers to high-performance computing clusters. We used hvantk for reanalysing three case-control cohorts, comprising congenital heart disease (CHD), developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Epi25) and schizophrenia (SCHEMA). Re-ranking of gene-based burden testing results using multi-omic annotations improved the recovery of curated disease genes from 26% to 49% in CHD, 40% to 48% in Epi25 and 51% to 54% in SCHEMA, among the top decile re-ranked genes. Expression at bulk and single-cell levels were the features contributing the most over a baseline of burden, gene constraint and publication count.

title: Multi-site real-world performance of commercial AI for pulmonary and incidental pulmonary embolism detection
desc: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality, yet the real-world performance of FDA-cleared AI detection models remains incompletely characterized. We retrospectively evaluated two FDA-cleared AI algorithms from a single commercial platform (Aidoc Medical BriefCase)—one for PE triage on dedicated CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA; n = 30,678) and one for incidental PE (iPE) detection on routine contrast-enhanced CTs ( n = 37,191), across a 17-facility academic health system. Reference-standard labels were extracted from radiology reports using a validated LLM pipeline (97% accuracy, κ = 0.94). The PE model achieved 86.8% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity, with sensitivity declining from 99.3% for saddle emboli to 72.9% for subsegmental PE, and from 89.7% for acute to 65.3% for non-acute PE. The iPE model achieved 73.5% sensitivity and 99.8% specificity. Both models demonstrated lower sensitivity than FDA-clearance benchmarks while exceeding cleared specificity, with diminishing performance for peripheral and non-acute emboli mirroring known human reader limitations and underscoring the need for standardized post-market surveillance of AI-enabled medical devices.

title: Opportunities and challenges of artificial intelligence and digital pathology in adult CNS tumors.
desc: [Journal of neuro-oncology] For over a century, the pathologist's interpretation at the microscope was the final word on a brain tumor's identity. The 2021 World Health Organization (WHO) classification of central nervous system (CNS) tumors, 5th edition, changed that hierarchy by introducing a layered, integrated diagnosis in which molecular findings take precedence over histology when the two conflict. Artificial intelligence (AI) applied to digitized slides adds a computational layer to this framework and marks a fundamental change in diagnostic workflow. This review examines the role of AI and digital pathology in adult CNS tumors and discusses the opportunities and challenges in clinical, neuro-oncology implementation. We conducted a narrative review of relevant literature indexed in PubMed before and after the 2021 WHO classification, covering digital pathology, whole-slide imaging (WSI), and AI applications in adult neuro-oncology. We synthesized evidence on diagnostic performance, molecular prediction, prognostic modeling, workflow integration, and ethical considerations. AI and digital pathology show potential to improve diagnostic consistency, shorten turnaround time, and integrate histopathological, molecular, and radiological information. AI models may support glioma grading, prediction of molecular alterations from routine histology, survival stratification, prediction of brain metastasis, and intraoperative decisions. Barriers to clinical adoption include limited generalizability, lack of transparency, data privacy, and evolving regulatory oversight. AI and digital pathology are transforming adult CNS tumor diagnostics and could improve precision, efficiency, and multidisciplinary decision-making. Successful implementation will require rigorous multi-institutional clinical validation, transparent governance, equitable access, and collaboration among patients and health care professionals.

title: Implicit reconstruction of gating strategies from sample-level flow cytometry annotations
desc: Flow cytometry is central to clinical hematology, generating extensive archives comprising billions of single-cell profiles linked to expert-derived diagnostic summaries. While these records represent a largely untapped repository of collective expert knowledge, the underlying single-cell annotations required for supervised machine learning are typically not recorded in a standardized, accessible format. We present IMPGAT (implicit gating), a weakly supervised multiple-instance learning framework that reconstructs single-cell gating strategies directly from existing sample-level cell-type frequency distributions. The model utilizes an induced set attention mechanism to map single-cell marker profiles to specific cell populations, requiring neither explicit cell-level labels nor unsupervised clustering during training. We evaluate the framework on acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cohorts, totaling 711 measurements from 268 individuals and 240 million single cells. In ALL, the model's quantification of cell-type abundances shows no statistically significant difference from human inter-expert variability. In AML, the framework achieves blast quantification on par with a recently established supervised state-of-the-art model that relies on explicit single-cell annotations for training. Error analysis shows that mismatches between model predictions and expert gating primarily involve expert-labeled non-cellular events, reflecting the non-incorporation of any explicit physical prior knowledge (such as the geometric relationships traditionally used to identify doublets and debris in scatter cytograms) in model training. Conversely, model certainty correlates with phenotypic borderline cases where manual bisection is inherently difficult. Our approach enables the systematic utilization of retrospective clinical records for the development of automated, standardized gating logic and is applicable to broader high-throughput contexts, such as large-scale immune monitoring or phenotypic drug screening.

title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI
desc: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians' ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors' internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.

title: GEO-BERT: A Retrieval augmented LLM Framework for Intelligent Dataset Retrieval from the Gene Expression Omnibus
desc: The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) is a commonly used data repository of high throughput gene expression and other functional genomics data. This platform is globally used by researchers for submitting experimental datasets, accessing these datasets for hypothesis validation, reusing them in data-driven research, generating ideas for new research directions. Despite global usage, searching and identifying relevant and usable datasets in GEO remains challenging with an underlying keyword based search system needing manual intervention for the retrieval of desired datasets. GEO's inconsistent metadata and varying data annotation practices across submissions, variable data quality are contributing to its challenge for building structured query tools. With the recent advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), it is timely to revisit the GEO datasets and its query system. Here, we present an AI chat-bot, GEO-BERT, leveraging an underlying retrieval augmented generator framework on the GEO metadata with a novel hierarchical hybrid field aware retrieval system to mine the datasets. GEO-BERT is locally installable, available for programmers and project developers (https://github.com/mrumi/GEOBERTtest) and readily usable by regular users on subset of test data. We demonstrated that GEO-BERT enhances the semantic search performance not currently available by any of the leading existing AI-powered chatbots, while improving the performance of GEO's traditional search performance for project development. Given the global usage of GEO and the latest advancement of the large language models, GEO-BERT fills the gap for context-aware extraction of GEO datasets.

title: Health misinformation and disinformation: Old narratives, new technologies.
source: PubMed · Advances in clinical and experimental medicine : official organ Wroclaw Medical University
desc: [Advances in clinical and experimental medicine : official organ Wroclaw Medical University] This editorial discusses how health misinformation and disinformation combine long-established narratives with new technologies that substantially increase the speed, reach, personalization, and apparent credibility of misleading content. The novelty of the contemporary information environment lies less in entirely new false narratives than in digital infrastructures that allow misleading content to be created, tailored, disseminated, and monetized at unprecedented scale. Online social media platforms and generative artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed these conditions, enabling misleading health information to be created and disseminated at previously impossible scale and speed. Health misinformation and disinformation can influence behavior, undermine trust in scientific and public health institutions, delay appropriate care, promote ineffective or harmful interventions, and weaken responses to disease outbreaks. Their effects may be particularly pronounced among populations with limited access to reliable information, healthcare, and trusted institutions. This editorial also examines how engagement-driven platform design, commercial and political incentives, synthetic media, and inconsistent safeguards amplify the problem. It argues that fact-checking and individual media literacy, while necessary, are insufficient on their own. A more effective response requires timely, transparent public health communication; institutional support for healthcare professionals; greater platform accountability; systematic safety evaluation of generative AI; independent access to relevant data; and policies that address the incentives sustaining the production and circulation of false and misleading health information.

desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Javier Pereira; conditions: Urinary Incontinence (UI); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 80; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The goal of this observational retrospective study is to characterize women with urinary incontinence and to identify factors associated with their response to treatment using artificial intelligence models. The main questions it aims to answer are: What are the clinical, functional, and therapeutic characteristics of women with urinary incontinence? Which clinical, functional, and lifestyle factors are associated with response to treatment? Can artificial intelligence models identify patterns and factors associated with treatment response? Researchers will analyze data from women with urinary incontinence collected during routine clinical care at a specialized pelvic floor clinic. The study will combine clinical information from medical records, measurements obtained from clinical assessment instruments, and daily-life data collected using wearable devices such as activity bracelets. Artificial intelligence and machine learning models will be applied to these data to characterize participants and identify factors associated with treatment response.

title: A Review of Suicide-Related Risks through Propensity Score Methods using the Maryland Suicide Data Warehouse
desc: Objective A diversity of approaches and cohorts have been published in research literature for suicide risk estimation, leading to some uncertainty around which factors and conditions are most strongly contributing to risk. Methods exist for weighting estimates by propensity score, removing simplifying the interpretation of model effects. Few studies have explored the use of these tools to assess when the effect of certain factors is uncertain or inconsistent. Method A mix of 1,001,737 suicide decedents and living patients were evaluated for suicide risk, relying on a subset of commonly identified factors: demographics, psychiatric conditions, substance use disorders, and social needs. Care utilization patterns were then assessed controlling for these factors in a hospital care setting. Four methods were considered for controlling multivariate confounding of odds predicting death by suicide: multivariate logistic regression, 1-to-1 sample matching, inverse propensity weighting (IPTW), and entropy balancing (EBAL). Results Test statistics showed suicide decedents were much more likely to have various psychiatric and substance use diagnoses, social needs and more likely to heightened care utilization across sampling intervals. Greater utilization was found close to date of death. Effect sizes after IPTW and EBAL weighting were also generally greater than would have been documented by regression alone. Conclusions Propensity weighting is a useful alternative to exploring nuanced effects, especially when the direction and strength of an association differ from traditional statistics. By weighting, the overall imbalance of cases remains consistent and effect terms might reflect more nuanced associations than regression or sample matching alone.

title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
desc: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

title: The Role of Environmental Information and the Limitations of Predictability with Transformer-based Time-Series Models for complex Astrocyte Trajectories
desc: Morphogenesis is the process by which an organism develops from a single cell into a complex organism, and one factor contributing to this complexity is the interaction between cells and their environment. In heterogeneous environments comprising differing cell types and polymeric structures, the observed complexity appears to approach an infinite value. Recent developments in imaging tools and deep learning for image analysis enable the extraction of meaning from terabyte-scale images at a realistic computational cost. In this paper, we used a Transformer-based model to predict the migration trajectories of astrocytes during mouse brain development, aiming to quantitatively elucidate (i) what makes prediction difficult, i.e., the structure of predictability and its theoretical limit, and (ii) to what extent environmental information (vascular structure) and multimodal modeling of the predictive distribution can improve prediction. Based on a bivariate Gaussian distribution ($mu, sigma, rho$) at each time point, we predicted future positions while accounting for uncertainty and evaluate the quality of the predictive distribution. We report three main findings. First, point-prediction accuracy reached a fundamental limit set by the irreducibility of the movement direction; the error curve was described with high accuracy by the mean-squared-displacement law of a persistent random walk. Second, extending the predictive distribution from a single bivariate Gaussian to a continuous mixture (mixture density network, MDN) captured the run/rest bimodality without discretization and substantially improved the quality of the predictive distribution (negative log-likelihood, NLL) while preserving point-prediction accuracy. Third, a model that integrated vascular environmental information into this multimodal model achieved the best performance in point-prediction accuracy, consistently across three training seeds, showing that environmental information contributes to prediction in combination with multimodal output. This study presents both an improvement of the predictive distribution for complex cell migration and a framework for quantifying the limit of predictability based on movement statistics.

Wavelet Scalogram-Based Nystagmus Classification for Automated Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo Subtype Diagnosis.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of vestibular vertigo, yet accurate diagnosis remains challenging without specialist expertise. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-based diagnostic algorithm for BPPV using video-nystagmography (VNG) recordings. A total of 1352 VNG recordings were collected from patients with posterior semicircular canal (PSCC) BPPV (n = 234), lateral semicircular canal (LSCC) BPPV (canalolithiasis, n = 188; cupulolithiasis, n = 58), and healthy controls (n = 224) at a single tertiary referral hospital, yielding 1738 signal segments (1312 nystagmus segments annotated by two otolaryngologists and 426 normal segments). Eye trajectory signals were extracted using a deep learning-based VNG eye-tracking algorithm, transformed into two-dimensional (2D) scalogram representations via continuous wavelet transform (CWT), and classified using task-specific backbone architectures selected through systematic comparison under a patient-level data split. Ablation analysis showed that CWT-based 2D representations significantly outperformed raw one-dimensional (1D) time-series baselines. The final models achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values of 0.974 for horizontal and 0.961 for torsional nystagmus classification. For BPPV subtype diagnosis, recording-level accuracy was 0.935 for the PSCC and 0.938 for the LSCC evaluation; F1-scores exceeded 0.84 for all PSCC classes and ranged from 0.59 to 0.98 for LSCC classes, with canalolithiasis variants outperforming cupulolithiasis variants. These findings suggest the feasibility of AI-assisted BPPV diagnosis from VNG recordings.

title: THE EFFECT OF A TRANSTHEORETICAL MODEL-BASED CHATBOT SUPPORT INTERVENTION ON SMOKING BEHAVIOR IN UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Seher DÖNER; conditions: Smoking ( Cigarette), Smoking (Tobacco) Addiction, Smoking Behaviors, Smoking Cessation, Tobacco Smoking; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 100; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The purpose of this clinical trial is to examine the impact of a chatbot-supported intervention based on the Transtheoretical Model (TTM) on smoking behavior, self-efficacy, decisional balance, and the urge to smoke among university students. The main questions it aims to answer are: * Does the chatbot-based support intervention, grounded in the Transtheoretical Model (TTM), have an effect on smoking behavior? * Does the chatbot-based support intervention, grounded in the Transtheoretical Model (TTM), have an effect on self-efficacy levels? * Does the chatbot-based support intervention, grounded in the Transtheoretical Model (TTM), have an effect on decisional balance? * Does the chatbot-based support intervention, grounded in the Transtheoretical Model (TTM), have an effect on the urge to smoke? The researchers will compare the experimental group with a group that received no intervention to determine whether the chatbot is effective in influencing smoking behavior. title: Normative Temperature, Demographic Categories, and the Limits of Infrared Thermometry
desc: Objective. Temperature readings are routinely stratified by race and ethnicity, though significant group differences may reflect physiology, instrument noise, or categorization rather than biology. This study tests whether these categories partition facial infrared thermography measurements beyond individual variation and baseline device noise. Approach. A secondary analysis of thermography data (n = 951 adults) compares inner-canthus maximum (TCEmax) and full-face maximum (Tmax) temperatures across five administrative categories via one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), mixed-effects modeling, Bland-Altman analysis against oral reference, and Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis. Main results. ANOVA returns significant group differences (p < 0.001; eta-squared = 0.04 for TCEmax, 0.03 for Tmax), but the total spread (0.2 to 0.3 degrees Celsius) is comparable to device accuracy and within-subject variability. Individual variation accounts for 95% of TCEmax variance, and adding simulated Gaussian noise to participant-level temperatures (sigma = 0.10 to 0.30 degrees Celsius) preserves the complete group-mean rank order in as few as 37.5% of iterations. Significance. Testing whether a group difference survives perturbation at the scale of instrument accuracy offers a check against treating significance alone as evidence of physiology. Here, observed group differences are small relative to measurement variability, and their physiological interpretation remains uncertain, with implications for clinical tools that treat administrative categories as biologically meaningful.

title: IECG: Weakly-Supervised Interpretability-Enhancing Foundation Model for Electrocardiogram
desc: Electrocardiography (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac diagnosis, yet most machine learning methods for ECG analysis lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. We present IECG, a weakly-supervised ECG foundation model that jointly performs diagnostic classification and abnormality localization without requiring manual abnormal region annotations, overcoming a long-standing bottleneck in interpretable ECG learning. Central to IECG is a weakly-supervised attention strategy that explicitly incorporates clinical priors by deriving abnormality heatmap pseudo-labels from established ECG clinical knowledge. These pseudo-labels guide the model's CLS-token attention through a KL-divergence loss, encouraging it to focus on diagnostically relevant waveform regions. During pretraining, IECG is jointly optimized with clinically guided attention supervision, ECG-text contrastive alignment, and report captioning objectives, enabling it to learn rich multimodal representations while producing localized waveform evidence. By explicitly aggregating features from clinically guided attention regions, IECG grounds its diagnostic predictions in interpretable waveform evidence without sacrificing classification performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IECG achieves state-of-the-art abnormal region localization while maintaining strong classification performance, advancing trustworthy foundation models for ECG analysis.

title: LoCoFlow: Local-Context Flow Matching for Single-Cell Dynamics and Fate Inference
desc: Single-cell sequencing profiles cellular states at discrete time points, providing population-level snapshots from which developmental and disease-associated trajectories can be reconstructed. Existing optimal-transport and flow-matching approaches typically infer temporal couplings at the level of individual cells, with limited representation of the local manifold geometry of cell-state space and the uncertainty inherent in lineage diversification. We introduce LoCoFlow, a flow-matching framework that combines local point-cloud geometry with conditional fate uncertainty. Overlapping patches define hierarchical transport between populations, and an endpoint-preserving neural bridge regularizes motion and deformation within these patches. Bridge velocities supervise a conditional field with patch-shared and cell-specific latent variables, from which alternative trajectories can be sampled without future observations. Temporal and spatial benchmarks show improvements in transport distance. On lineage-traced LARRY data, LoCoFlow reduces mean raw Brier error from 0.7990 to 0.6620 relative to scDiffEq at the same number of endpoint draws. Expression perturbations further reveal distinct roles for focal-cell and neighborhood information: geometric-patch models show aligned background and whole-patch responses, whereas random-minibatch models show opposing focal and background responses. These findings support local context as a useful representation for probabilistic fate inference and provide testable hypotheses about how it shapes predicted responses.

source: PubMed · Zhongguo fei ai za zhi = Chinese journal of lung cancer
desc: [Zhongguo fei ai za zhi = Chinese journal of lung cancer] Lung cancer remains the malignant tumor with the highest incidence and mortality rates worldwide, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of cases. Radical surgical resection serves as the primary curative modality for patients with resectable NSCLC; however, postoperative recurrence persists in a subset of patients, thereby compromising long-term survival outcomes. Consequently, the precise prediction of postoperative recurrence risk, identification of high-risk populations, and formulation of individualized adjuvant therapy and surveillance strategies are of paramount importance for improving patient prognosis. In recent years, fueled by the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and liquid biopsy technologies, the prediction of postoperative recurrence in NSCLC has progressively transitioned toward greater precision and personalization. This review summarizes the current applications of traditional predictive models, AI-based models, and liquid biopsy techniques in forecasting NSCLC recurrence following surgery, evaluating their respective strengths and limitations. Furthermore, it provides insights into future research trajectories. .

title: Block Diffusion for Longitudinal EHR: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Representation Trade-offs
desc: Autoregressive (AR) models have proved effective for zero-shot prediction from longitudinal electronic health records, but impose strictly sequential generation on trajectories containing temporally clustered and interdependent clinical events. We investigate block-based masked diffusion (BD) as an alternative on MIMIC-IV under matched tokenisation, context length, model capacity, and evaluation conditions. Across block sizes, BD exhibits a clear quality--efficiency trade-off, with small-block configurations retaining much of the predictive performance of AR while enabling substantially faster inference. A representative $B{=}8$ configuration achieves approximately $1.43\times$ faster evaluation. Although generative rollout remains below AR in most settings, frozen linear probes on BD and AR representations achieve near-identical performance across clinical prediction tasks, indicating that BD learns comparably informative clinical representations. Increasing the denoising budget yields diminishing returns, while alternative decoding strategies provide limited gains. Overall, our results show that block diffusion is a viable and computationally attractive approach to longitudinal EHR modelling, with further improvements in iterative decoding offering a promising route toward closing the remaining generative performance gap.

title: Bypassing Current Biosecurity Screens with AI Designed Proteins and Closing the Gap with Edge-AI Functional Screening
desc: DNA synthesis machines are vital tools in medicine and research, but they can be misused to produce sequences which are transcribed and translated to produce toxic proteins. Synthesis providers may screen orders for dangerous sequences, but most screening software performs sequence-based alignment, which is vulnerable to AI redesign attacks. Additionally, software-only synthesis screening requires the operator of the machine to be trusted. We present Capiti, an edge-deployed screening system that runs with no internet connection, listens directly to a synthesizer's valve control signals, and aborts a run when it detects incipient pathogenic function. Rather than performing sequence alignment, Capiti is specifically trained to recognize fold. ProteinMPNN was used to generate putatively functional variants of known pathogenic proteins, and a CNN was trained to separate them from active-site knockouts, scrambles, and decoys. We release two models, Capiti-E (known pathogenic proteins) and Capiti-C (resistance genes for antibiotics of last resort), alongside emusynth, a DNA synthesizer emulator. On our test sets, IBBIS commec and SeqScreen incorrectly passed 18.5% and 44.7% of putatively functional pathogenic variants respectively; Capiti passed 0.24%.

desc: [Frontiers in physiology] This study aimed to characterize the development landscape of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted tongue diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) by comparing publication trends, collaboration patterns, research hotspots, and emerging topics between CNKI-indexed and WoSCC-indexed literature. Literature published between January 2015 and August 2026 was retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). Publication trends were summarized descriptively, and CiteSpace and VOSviewer were used for collaboration-network, keyword co-occurrence, clustering, timeline, burst-detection, and journal citation analyses. CNKI-indexed and WoSCC-indexed records were analysed separately because of differences in database coverage, indexing characteristics, metadata structures, and publication practices. A total of 482 studies were included, comprising 295 WoSCC-indexed and 187 CNKI-indexed records. Publication output showed an overall upward trend in both datasets over the study period. The CNKI keyword clustering network showed high clustering quality (modularity Q = 0.7929; weighted mean silhouette S = 0.9413), as did the WoSCC network (Q = 0.8000; S = 0.9239). In CNKI, the strongest keyword bursts included "deep learning" (strength = 2.95), "image segmentation" (2.69), and "transfer learning" (2.61); in WoSCC, prominent bursts included "artificial intelligence" (2.13), "image colour analysis" (2.10), and "machine learning" (1.86). CNKI-indexed literature showed prominent themes involving tongue-image objectification, segmentation, and TCM-oriented diagnostic concepts, whereas WoSCC-indexed literature showed more differentiated themes involving AI architectures, tongue-feature analysis, computational modelling, and disease-related applications. Highly cited publications in both datasets further reflected the importance of tongue-image extraction and segmentation and the subsequent expansion toward disease-oriented modelling. Across both datasets, the temporal patterns suggested a shift in research attention from conventional image processing and feature extraction toward machine learning, deep learning, and more integrated AI-based approaches. The two datasets showed complementary but database-specific thematic structures in AI-assisted tongue diagnosis. title: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?
desc: Masked language modelling (MLM) is the dominant pretraining objective for transformer encoders applied to longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). However, reconstructing individual events may overemphasise noisy or weakly informative observations and does not explicitly encourage learning higher-level patient states. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) instead learn by predicting representations in latent space and have shown strong performance in a variety of domains. In this paper, we investigate to what extent JEPA can be adapted to EHR sequence representation. Our empirical investigation using MIMIC-IV shows that although all three of our JEPA formulations train stably without representational collapse, they consistently underperform standard MLM. We find that target size, not target heterogeneity, increases prediction error, yet reducing the target size does not recover downstream performance. This suggests that stable latent prediction alone is insufficient for competitive EHR representation learning and highlights the challenge of defining clinically meaningful latent targets for EHR.

title: In Other Words: Learning When to Trust Generated Protein Function Descriptions
desc: Generative protein-to-text models write function descriptions in free-form English but give no indication of which to believe. Indeed, free text is hard to evaluate. We introduce a large language model judge of equivalence of predicted vs. ''true'' function descriptions, validated against blinded expert curation. We also present ProtTale, our sequence-to-text model, that learns from the judge's verdicts to estimate its own reliability, pJay. On unseen Swiss-Prot enzymes, ProtTale and three other leading methods tie on accuracy but are right about different proteins. Here, ProtTale's unique correct predictions outnumber all other methods' combined. Scored from sequence alone, pJay is a plug-in filter, raising all models' performance. On short proteins, it raises precision for every tested method nearly twofold. We argue that generative annotation becomes useful not by being right more often, but by knowing when it can be trusted---a standard that every generative model in biology should meet.

Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging in the diagnosis and assessment of Parkinson's disease.
desc: [Frontiers in neurology] Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized primarily by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc); noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC) are also frequently affected. Because clinical motor symptoms usually emerge only after substantial neurodegeneration has occurred, there is a compelling need for noninvasive imaging biomarkers capable of detecting early pathological changes. Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (NM-MRI) generates neuromelanin-related image contrast in the SNpc and LC and can indirectly reflect the structural integrity of these catecholaminergic nuclei. Current evidence suggests that NM-MRI may be useful for distinguishing patients with PD from healthy controls, supporting the differential diagnosis of selected atypical parkinsonian syndromes and essential tremor, assessing disease stage, monitoring longitudinal change, and evaluating high-risk individuals in the prodromal phase. This review provides an updated account of recent advances in the use of NM-MRI for diagnostic support, differential diagnosis, prodromal assessment, longitudinal monitoring, multimodal imaging, and artificial intelligence-based analysis, and discusses its clinical role relative to other imaging and fluid biomarkers. Combining NM-MRI with complementary imaging measures, such as quantitative susceptibility mapping and diffusion MRI, and with automated analytical methods may further enhance pathological characterization and quantitative assessment. However, the available evidence is derived largely from single-center or case-control studies with limited sample sizes. Substantial variability may arise from differences in scanners, magnetic field strengths, acquisition protocols, and analytical methods, while independent external validation and prospective multicenter longitudinal evidence remain limited. The biological basis of the NM-MRI signal has not been fully established, and artificial intelligence models developed for NM-MRI remain vulnerable to overfitting, limited interpretability, and limited cross-center generalizability. Accordingly, NM-MRI cannot currently serve as a stand-alone diagnostic tool for PD or replace diagnosis based on comprehensive clinical assessment.
