title: Reading the Mask: Descriptor-Grounded BI-RADS Rationale Generation for Breast MRI Segmentation
desc: Deep learning based models accurately delineate tumours on dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), but segmentation masks alone do not provide the rationales or reasoning used by radiologists to assess the lesion suspicion. This limits the explainability as well the clinical integration. We investigate whether clinically relevant descriptors can instead be derived from the segmentation masks and their dynamic contrast-enhancement series. We have used Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) guidelines as a structured framework. Using these guidelines we designed a BI-RADS decision tree with eight quantitative measurements using radiomics, together with the lesion size and component count, that determine the descriptors at eight nodes. Using these descriptors we generate natural-language rationale using a large language model. The model was constrained to express only the derived records from the decision tree. After applying this framework to the expert and automatic masks of each of the 1,506 cases in the MAMA-MIA dataset, we generated a reproducible corpus of 3,012 BI-RADS grounded rationales. We obtained a faithfulness score of 99.98% and a counterfactual accuracy of 99.3%, indicating that the generated rationales faithfully verbalises the measured descriptors and correctly reflects changes in the underlying record. Agreement between the descriptors from expert and automatic masks falls from 0.832 to 0.549 as mask quality falls from Good to Missed. The generated rationales are intended as draft representations for radiologist review and final sign-off rather than autonomous clinical reports.

title: Going beyond labels: Semi-supervised learning for enzyme kinetic parameter prediction
desc: Enzyme kinetic parameters, such as the turnover number (kcat), underpin enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling. Machine learning models can predict these parameters from sequence and substrate representations, but their accuracy is limited by the scarcity and narrow coverage of experimentally labeled data, particularly for out-of-distribution enzymes. Existing strategies to exploit unlabeled data rely on homologous sequences, pseudo-labels or synthetic perturbations of labeled samples, limiting their potential to fully leverage unlabeled data for model improvement. Here, we show that regularization-based semi-supervised learning improves model performance by leveraging biologically meaningful unlabeled samples alongside labeled data during task-specific training, without assigning pseudo-labels to the unlabeled samples. Specifically, enzyme-substrate pairs lacking kcat, but characterized for other kinetic parameters, can serve as unlabeled data that improve kcat prediction. Using the clustered CataPro dataset at 40% sequence identity as a stringent benchmark, neural consistency regularization and graph-Laplacian regularization each performed better when unlabeled records were added, beyond the gains from regularization on labeled data alone. The benefit required sufficient labeled data, saturated at a few thousand unlabeled records for the neural model, and depended on the density of the unlabeled data in the feature space rather than on their proximity to labeled data. Gains extended to wild-type and mutant enzymes and to a local low-data adenylate kinase landscape. These findings show that incomplete kinetic records specifically, and unlabeled data points generally, are a valuable resource for enzyme kinetics prediction.

source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] AI-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSSs) can help primary care clinicians provide higher quality care amid rising case complexity and resource constraints. However, evidence regarding their effectiveness and safety in primary care practice is lacking. We synthesized evidence on the effectiveness and safety of AI-CDSSs compared with usual care or non-AI-based systems in primary care settings. We conducted a systematic review following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and reported the results according to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines. We included experimental and quasi-experimental studies evaluating AI-CDSSs used by health care professionals in primary care settings, compared with usual care or non-AI-based decision support systems, and that reported clinician-, patient-, or system-level outcomes, or safety. An information specialist designed the search strategies and systematically reviewed MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from inception to June 27, 2025. Reviewers independently performed the selection and extraction processes. Data extraction was informed by the DECIDE-AI and CONSORT-AI (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials-AI) reporting guidelines and the APPRAISE-AI tool. We independently assessed the risk of bias using Risk of Bias-2 or Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, we conducted a synthesis without meta-analysis and explored heterogeneity using an adapted Non-Adoption, Abandonment, Scale-Up, Spread, and Sustainability-informed implementation-context classification. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251119225). We identified 4074 records through database searches and 12 additional records through citation searching and trial registration checking. We included 14 records on 11 distinct studies, including 4 experimental and 7 quasi-experimental studies. The risk of bias was high in all experimental studies and serious to critical in quasi-experimental studies. AI-CDSSs showed more consistent positive effects on workflow-related outcomes in structured and protocolized decision contexts, particularly for screening, referral, and alert optimization tasks. title: Clinical radar heart sounds with echocardiographic phenotypes of ventricular dysfunction and valvular disease
desc: Radar heart sounds capture cardiac mechanical activity without contact, while echocardiography characterizes ventricular and valvular function. Paired measurements connect these signals to structural heart disease, yet such data remain sparsely represented in public resources. Here we present 537 radar heart-sound recordings paired with one echocardiographic report for each of 162 patients. The cohort covers three overlapping phenotypes: left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 50%, regional wall-motion abnormality and at least moderate valvular regurgitation, present in 38, 43 and 39 patients, respectively. Original complex signals, processed radar heart sounds and temporal quality segmentation support signal-to-phenotype analysis. Technical validation retains 95.93% of signal duration and confirms reproducible waveform reconstruction. Patient-level five-fold evaluation achieves a mean outer-test AUROC of $0.770\pm0.138$ for reduced LVEF, identifying mechanical information associated with ventricular systolic dysfunction. This resource supports research linking non-contact cardiac mechanical signals to echocardiographic structural and functional phenotypes.

title: G-ALN: a GPU-accelerated BWA-aln algorithm for palaeogenomics
desc: Abstract Summary: The most commonly used method to achieve optimal mapping for short and damaged ancient DNA (aDNA) reads is the BWA-aln algorithm with seeding disabled. However, this CPU-based algorithm is computationally demanding, as the aligner must tolerate mismatches and indels across the entire read. To improve alignment speed, we present G-ALN: a GPU implementation of the BWA-aln and indexing algorithms. G-ALN first searches all reads on GPU cores, with reads that need a long search being shared dynamically between the GPU and any spare CPU cores. Every read is searched using the same algorithm as BWA, so the output is byte-identical, which we confirmed here using woolly mammoth and Neanderthal datasets with aDNA-specific parameters. In our benchmarking, G-ALN indexed a reference genome ~32 times faster than BWA, and read alignment speed increased ~6-fold. G-ALN was developed through AI-assisted coding (Claude Opus 5.5). It processes thousands of reads in parallel on each GPU and aligns more than twice as many aDNA reads per unit of energy. These results show that G-ALN offers a practical route to using GPU resources in established aDNA analysis workflows. Availability and Implementation: G-ALN is implemented in C++ and CUDA and is freely available under the GPLv3 license at https://github.com/bilalbioinfo/galn. It requires an NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 7.0 or higher and CUDA 11.8 or later.

[Artificial Intelligence in Acute Ischemic Stroke:Time-Oriented Diagnostic Support and Treatment Prediction].
source: PubMed · No shinkei geka. Neurological surgery
desc: [No shinkei geka. Neurological surgery] Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used in acute ischemic stroke. Their clinical value depends not only on diagnostic accuracy but also on whether these systems improve time-critical decision-making. Current applications include prehospital triage, detection of large-vessel and medium-vessel occlusions, automated ASPECTS assessment, estimation of ischemic core and penumbra, collateral evaluation, and workflow notification using CT, CT angiography, CT perfusion, and MRI. AI is also being investigated to predict treatment response, futile recanalization, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, brain edema, and final infarct volume after reperfusion therapy. In clinical practice, prognostic prediction must be distinguished from treatment-effect prediction. Useful AI systems should report uncertainty and calibration and provide actionable outputs at the clinically relevant time point while remaining embedded in a human-in-the-loop workflow. Future multimodal platforms may integrate imaging, clinical data, transfer information, procedure-related variables, and device characteristics to support individualized acute stroke workflows and endovascular procedural planning.

title: From Canon to Nikon: Camera Domain Shift and Potential Equity Implications in Retinal AI
desc: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness, yet access to regular screening remains limited worldwide. AI offers a scalable approach, but its performance can be sensitive to image quality and acquisition conditions. In a Brazilian cohort of 8,524 patients, retinal images acquired with the Nikon NF5050 were more than twice as likely to have inadequate image quality compared with those acquired with the Canon CR-2, despite refurbished Canon systems costing more than twice as much as Nikon systems. This potential cost-quality trade-off highlights an important consideration for the reliability of AI systems deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. Using a frozen pretrained retinal foundation model, we systematically evaluate whether camera-associated performance differences persist across 12 retinal disease classification tasks, four input resolutions, and five downstream classifiers. We find that camera-associated performance differences vary substantially across tasks, and that neither higher input resolution nor classifier choice consistently mitigates cross-camera variation. These findings identify camera platform as a potentially overlooked source of performance variability, with implications for the safety and reliability of retinal AI when deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. We release all source code, evaluation scripts, and per-task results on GitHub to support reproducible benchmarking.

title: Evaluation of object detection neural networks to find topologically associated domains in bulk Hi-C data
desc: Topologically associated domains (TADs) shape the three-dimensional structure of chromatin and contribute to gene regulation by arranging regulatory elements and genes in spatial proximity. This spatial proximity is captured by Hi-C, an experimental method, which quantifies contact frequencies between all pairs of genomic loci. In bulk Hi-C data, TADs can be found in the form of gapped, nested and partially overlapping squares centered on the main diagonal of the Hi-C matrix. We shift the problem of TAD identification into the domain of computer vision by detecting TADs in Hi-C in the form of squares in images. For this we use object detection, which aims to classify object instances in images. This study evaluates the applicability of the object detection neural networks YOLOv8 and Mask R-CNN on the identification of TADs in bulk Hi-C data. We build image-like data from Hi-C matrices, predict reference TADs with a state-of-the-art TAD caller, train the models and evaluate the detections. Our results confirm that YOLOv8 and Mask R-CNN learn to detect reference TADs, new TADs and overlapping TADs (although absent in training data). All three show increased ChIP-Seq signal of the TAD-associated factors CTCF, RAD21 and H3K4me3 on their boundaries, emphasizing their biological reliability. Comparisons with reference TADs indicate that Mask R-CNN detects more TADs with less precise positioning, while YOLOv8 detects fewer TADs with lower nesting complexity but improved positioning.
